label: thmA
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: def:real
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:real}
An $R$-module $M$ is \emph{real} if for all $m_1,\dots,m_k\in M$,
\[\textstyle\sum_im_i\otimes m_i=0\ \text{ in }M\otimes_RM\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_i=0\ \text{ for all }i.\]
A submodule $N\subseteq M$ is \emph{real} if $M/N$ is a real module. A \emph{real prime submodule} is a prime submodule which is real, and $M$ is \emph{semireal} if it has a proper real submodule.
head: environment

label: thmB
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:basic
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) If $N$ is a prime submodule then for every $0 \ne \bar{m} \in M/N$ and every $r \in  \operatorname{Ann}_R(\bar m)$ we have $m \not\in N$ and $rm \in N$ which implies $rM \subseteq N$; i.e. $r \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M/N)$. The reverse inclusion always holds; so $M/N$ is a prime module. Conversely, if $M/N$ is a prime module then for every $r \in R$ 
and $m \in M$ such that $rm \in N$ we have $r\bar{m}=0$ in $M/N$ which implies that either $\bar{m}=0$ 
or $r \in  \operatorname{Ann}_R(\bar m)=\operatorname{Ann}_R(M/N)$; i.e. either $m \in N$ or $rM \subseteq N$.

(b) For $m\in M$ put $I_m:=(N:m)=\operatorname{Ann}_R(\bar m)$; it depends only on $\bar m$. Since $I_m(M/N)$ is the image of $I_m M$ in $M/N$, we have
$\bar m\in I_m(M/N)$ if and only if $m\in I_mM+N.$
Hence $M/N$ is a semiprime module if and only if ($*$) $m\in I_mM+N$ implies $m\in N$, whereas $N$ is a semiprime submodule if and only if ($**$) $m\in I_mM$ implies $m\in N$. Clearly ($*$) implies ($**$). Conversely, assume ($**$) and let $m=m'+n$ with $m'\in I_mM$ and $n\in N$. Then $\bar m'=\bar m$, so $I_{m'}=I_m$ and $m'\in I_{m'}M$; by ($**$), $m'\in N$, hence $m\in N$.

(c) If $M$ is prime and $q\neq0$, then $\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)M=\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)M=0\not\ni q$; with (a) and (b) this shows that prime submodules are semiprime.

(d) If $N=\bigcap_iN_i$, then $(N:m)\subseteq(N_i:m)$, so $m\in(N:m)M$ implies $m\in N_i$ for every $i$.

(e) Let $L\subseteq M$. If $M$ is semiprime and $q\in L$ satisfies $q\in\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)L$, then $q\in\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)M$, so $q=0$. If $M$ is prime and $L\neq0$, then for $0\neq m\in L$ we have $\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}_R(L)\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}_R(m)=\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)$, so $\operatorname{Ann}_R(m)=\operatorname{Ann}_R(L)$ for all $0\neq m\in L$.

(f) Let $M=\prod_\alpha M_\alpha$ with all $M_\alpha$ semiprime, and let $q=\sum_jb_jy_j$ with $b_j\in\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)$ and $y_j\in M$. For each $\alpha$, the $\alpha$-component $q_\alpha=\sum_jb_j(y_j)_\alpha$ lies in $\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)M_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}_R(q_\alpha)M_\alpha$, so $q_\alpha=0$; hence $q=0$. Direct sums are submodules of direct products; apply (e).

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~ef{lem:basic}(b), $(N:m)=\operatorname{Ann}_R( ar m)$, and $N$ is semiprime if and only if $Q:=M/N$ is.

(a) If $r^2q=0$, then $r\in\operatorname{Ann}_R(rq)$, so $rq\in\operatorname{Ann}_R(rq)Q$, implying $rq=0$. Thus $\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)$ is radical. 

(b) Suppose that $0

The ideal $IR_\mathfrak p$ is nonzero and contained in $\mathfrak p R_\mathfrak p$, so $IR_\mathfrak p=(\pi^k)$ for some $k\ge1$; moreover $IR_\mathfrak p$ is radical, because $I$ is radical and localization preserves radical ideals, whence $IR_\mathfrak p=(\pi)$. label: lem:minprime
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Put $A:=R/I$ and $P:=\mathfrak p/I$. The primes of $A_P=(R/I)_\mathfrak p$ correspond to the primes $\mathfrak q$ of $R$ with $I\subseteq\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak p$, so by minimality $A_P$ has exactly one prime, its maximal ideal $PA_P$. Write $ ar a$ for the image of $a\in R$ in $A$; the elements of $A_P$ are the fractions $ ar a/ ar s$ with $a\in R$ and $s
otin\mathfrak p$. Since $I$ is radical, $A$ is reduced, and so is $A_P$: if $( ar a/ ar s)^n=0$, then $ ar u ar a^n=0$ for some $u
otin\mathfrak p$, so $( ar u ar a)^n=0$, hence $ ar u ar a=0$ and $ ar a/ ar s=0$. The nilradical of $A_P$ is the intersection of all primes of $A_P$, which is $PA_P$; since $A_P$ is reduced, the nilradical is zero, so $PA_P=0$. As $PA_P$ is the maximal ideal of $A_P$, it follows that $A_P$ is a field. For $a\in\mathfrak p$ we get $ ar a/ ar1\in PA_P=0$, i.e.\ $ ar t ar a=0$ for some $t
otin\mathfrak p$, which means $ta\in I$.

(b) If $\sum_ia_i^2\in\mathfrak p$, then by (a) there is $t
otin\mathfrak p$ with $t\sum_ia_i^2\in I$, so $\sum_i(ta_i)^2\in I$, whence $ta_i\in I\subseteq\mathfrak p$ and $a_i\in\mathfrak p$.

head: environment
name: A decomposition

label: ex:freeinf
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:freeinf}
Let $R=k[x,y]$, $\mathfrak m=(x,y)$, $M=R^{(\mathbb N)}$ with basis $e_0,e_1,\dots$, and
\[N:=\{f\in M:\ \textstyle\sum_nf_n\in(x)\ \text{and}\ f_n\in\mathfrak m\ \text{for all }n\}.\]
Let $V:=k^{(\mathbb N_{\ge1})}$, on which $R$ acts through $R/\mathfrak m$. The map\[\varphi:M\to k[y]\oplus V,\qquad f\mapsto\bigl((\textstyle\sum_nf_n)(0,y),\ (f_n(0,0))_{n\ge1}\bigr),\]is $R$-linear and surjective with kernel $N$ (the two conditions also force $f_0\in\mathfrak m$), so $M/N\cong k[y]\oplus V$. This quotient is semiprime by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(f), since $k[y]\cong R/(x)$ and $V\cong(R/\mathfrak m)^{(\mathbb N_{\ge1})}$ are prime, hence semiprime, modules. It is not prime, since $\operatorname{Ann}_R(1,0)=(x)\neq\mathfrak m=\operatorname{Ann}_R(0,v)$ for $0\neq v\in V$. The minimal primes over the annihilators are $(x)$ and $\mathfrak m$, and
\[K(N,(x))=\{f:\ \textstyle\sum_nf_n\in(x)\},\qquad K(N,\mathfrak m)=\mathfrak mM:\]
for the first, note $N+xM=N$; if $\sum_nf_n\in(x)$, then $yf\in N$, since $\sum_nyf_n=y\sum_nf_n\in(x)$ and each $yf_n\in\mathfrak m$, and conversely $sf\in N$ with $s\notin(x)$ gives $s\sum_nf_n\in(x)$, hence $\sum_nf_n\in(x)$; for the second, note $N+\mathfrak mM=\mathfrak mM$, and every $s\notin\mathfrak m$ acts invertibly on $M/\mathfrak mM$. Hence $N=K(N,(x))\cap K(N,\mathfrak m)$ is the decomposition of Theorem~\ref{thmA}. Note that the quotient $M/N\cong k[y]\oplus V$ happens to be a direct sum of cyclic modules. Here $R$ is not a Dedekind domain, and $M$ and $N$ are not finitely generated, so none of \cite[Theorem~1]{C22a}, \cite[Corollary~13]{JS} and \cite[Theorem~2.6]{Ary} applies.

label: lem:realbasic
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Let $L$ be a submodule of a real module $M$, with inclusion $j:L\to M$. If $\sum_ix_i\otimes x_i=0$ in $L\otimes L$, applying $j\otimes j$ gives $\sum_ix_i\otimes x_i=0$ in $M\otimes M$, so $x_i=0$ for all $i$.

(b) Let $M=\prod_\alpha M_\alpha$ with all $M_\alpha$ real, and let $\pi_\alpha:M\to M_\alpha$ be the projections. If $\sum_ix_i\otimes x_i=0$ in $M\otimes M$, then applying $\pi_\alpha\otimes\pi_\alpha$ gives $\sum_i\pi_\alpha(x_i)\otimes\pi_\alpha(x_i)=0$ in $M_\alpha\otimes M_\alpha$, so $\pi_\alpha(x_i)=0$ for all $\alpha$, i.e.\ $x_i=0$. Direct sums are submodules of direct products; apply (a).

(c) If $N=\bigcap_\alpha N_\alpha$ with all $N_\alpha$ real, the canonical maps $M/N\to M/N_\alpha$ induce an embedding $M/N\hookrightarrow\prod_\alpha M/N_\alpha$; apply (b) and (a).

(d) If $q\in\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)M$, say $q=\sum_jb_jy_j$ with $b_jq=0$, then $q\otimes q=\sum_jy_j\otimes b_jq=0$, so $q=0$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(b).
head: environment

label: lem:Kreal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Kreal}
Let $\mathfrak p$ be a real prime ideal and let $N$ be a submodule of an $R$-module $M$. Then $K(N,\mathfrak p)$ is a real submodule of $M$; hence, if $K(N,\mathfrak p)\neq M$, it is a real prime submodule with $(K(N,\mathfrak p):M)=\mathfrak p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $D:=R/\mathfrak p$, $F:=\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ and $Q':=M/K(N,\mathfrak p)$; write $\bar r$ for the image of $r\in R$ in $D$. Every element of $F$ has the form $\bar r/\bar s$ with $r\in R$, $s\notin\mathfrak p$.

\emph{$F$ is formally real.} If $\sum_i(\bar a_i/\bar s)^2=0$, then $\sum_ia_i^2\in\mathfrak p$, so all $a_i\in\mathfrak p$ because $\mathfrak p$ is real, i.e.\ all $\bar a_i/\bar s=0$.

\emph{$Q'$ embeds into an $F$-vector space.} If $K(N,\mathfrak p)=M$, then $Q'=0$ is real. Otherwise $K(N,\mathfrak p)$ is a prime submodule with $(K(N,\mathfrak p):M)=\mathfrak p$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:Np}(a), so $Q'$ is a torsion-free $D$-module by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(a) (cf.\ \cite[Lemma~1]{JS}). Hence $Q'$ embeds into its localization $V:=S^{-1}Q'$ at $S:=D\setminus\{0\}$, which is an $F$-vector space on which $R$ acts through $R\to D\subseteq F$.

\emph{$V$ is a real $R$-module.} We first show $V\otimes_RV=V\otimes_DV=V\otimes_FV$, via $v\otimes w\mapsto v\otimes w$. Since $\mathfrak p V=0$, also $\mathfrak p(V\otimes_RV)=0$, so $V\otimes_RV$ is a $D$-module. As $R\to D$ is surjective, a map $V\times V\to X$ into a $D$-module $X$ is $R$-bilinear if and only if it is $D$-bilinear; so $V\otimes_RV$ has the universal property of $V\otimes_DV$, i.e.\ $V\otimes_RV=V\otimes_DV$. Next, every element of $F$ has the form $ds^{-1}$ with $d\in D$ and $0\neq s\in D$, and for $v,w\in V$ we get in $V\otimes_DV$, using $D$-bilinearity for the scalar $s\in D$,
\[(s^{-1}v)\otimes w=(s^{-1}v)\otimes s(s^{-1}w)=s(s^{-1}v)\otimes(s^{-1}w)=v\otimes(s^{-1}w).\]
So the $D$-bilinear map $V\times V\to V\otimes_DV$ is $F$-bilinear, and $V\otimes_DV=V\otimes_FV$. If $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i=0$, choose a basis $w_1,\dots,w_r$ of a finite-dimensional subspace containing all $v_i$ and write $v_i=\sum_jv_{ij}w_j$; the coefficient of $w_j\otimes w_j$ gives $\sum_iv_{ij}^2=0$ in $F$, so all $v_{ij}=0$ and all $v_i=0$.

Since $Q'$ is isomorphic to a submodule of $V$, it is real by Lemma~\ref{lem:realbasic}(a), i.e.\ $K(N,\mathfrak p)$ is a real submodule. The last statement now follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Np}(a).

label: prop:realann
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $(N:m)=\operatorname{Ann}_R(\bar m)$, and $N$ is real if and only if $Q:=M/N$ is real.

(a) If $\sum_ia_i^2\in\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)$, then $\sum_i(a_iq)\otimes(a_iq)=\bigl((\sum_ia_i^2)q\bigr)\otimes q=0$, so $a_iq=0$ for all $i$.

(b) By Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(b), $Q$ is semiprime. For $0\neq q\in Q$, let $\mathfrak p$ be a minimal prime over $\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)$. Then $\mathfrak p$ is real by Lemma~\ref{lem:minprime}(b), and $q\notin K(0,\mathfrak p)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:key}. Hence $0=\bigcap_{\mathfrak p\text{ real}}K(0,\mathfrak p)$ in $Q$, an intersection of real submodules (Lemma~\ref{lem:Kreal}), so $Q$ is real by Lemma~\ref{lem:realbasic}(c).

(c) Real ideals are radical, so $N$ is semiprime by Proposition~\ref{rem:dauns}(b); apply (b).

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Let $m\notin N$ and $Q:=M/N$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:realbasic}(d) and Proposition~\ref{prop:realann}(a), $Q$ is semiprime and $\operatorname{Ann}_R(\bar m)$ is a real, hence radical, ideal. Let $\mathfrak p$ be a minimal prime over $\operatorname{Ann}_R(\bar m)$. Then $\mathfrak p$ is real (Lemma~\ref{lem:minprime}(b)), and $m\notin K(N,\mathfrak p)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:key}.
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii): each $K(N,\mathfrak p)\neq M$ is a real prime submodule by Lemma~\ref{lem:Kreal}.
(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i): Lemma~\ref{lem:realbasic}(c).

For the consequences, note first that the real submodules containing $N$ are closed under intersections (Lemma~\ref{lem:realbasic}(c)), and that each of them is an intersection of real prime submodules containing $N$. Next, if a proper submodule $N$ of $M$ is real, then (iii) provides a real prime submodule containing $N$; conversely, a real prime submodule is proper. Finally, if $N$ is maximal among the proper real submodules, every real prime submodule containing $N$ equals $N$, and there is at least one.
head: environment

label: ex:cyclic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:cyclic}
(1) Since $R/I\otimes_RR/I=R/I$, the module $R/I$ is real if and only if $I$ is a real ideal. Thus $\mathbb Z/p$ is prime but not real, since $1^2+\dots+1^2$ ($p$ terms) lies in $p\mathbb Z$, and for the prime ideal $I=(x^2+y^2+1)$ of $\mathbb R[x,y]$ the module $\mathbb R[x,y]/I$ is prime but not real, as $-1$ is a sum of squares in it. So real modules form a proper subclass of semiprime modules.

(2) If $R$ is real, then every free module $R^{(I)}$ is real by Lemma~\ref{lem:realbasic}(b), hence so is every submodule of a free module, in particular every projective module (Lemma~\ref{lem:realbasic}(a)); for instance, every projective module over $\mathbb R[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ is real.

(3) If $R$ is a principal ideal domain, then an $R$-module $M$ is real if and only if $\operatorname{Ann}_R(q)$ is a real ideal for every $q\in M$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:realann}(a),(c). For $R=\mathbb Z$ the only real ideals are $0$ and $\mathbb Z$, so an abelian group is real if and only if it is torsion-free.

otin(x-a)$ and $sq\in(x-a)M$, then the $a$-component of $sq$ is $0$; as $s$ acts on $R/(x-a)\cong\mathbb R[y]$ as the nonzero polynomial $s(a,y)$, the $a$-component of $q$ is $0$. head: environment
name: A decomposition into real primes

label: lem:tensorM
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tensorM}
Let $N$ be a submodule of an $R$-module $M$. Then $N$ is real if and only if $\sum_im_i\otimes m_i\in\operatorname{im}(M\otimes N+N\otimes M\to M\otimes M)$ implies $m_i\in N$ for all $i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $Q:=M/N$. Let $\pi:M\to Q$ be the quotient map, and let $L\subseteq M\otimes M$ be the submodule generated by all $m\otimes n$ and $n\otimes m$ with $m\in M$, $n\in N$; this is $\operatorname{im}(M\otimes N+N\otimes M\to M\otimes M)$. We claim that $\ker(\pi\otimes\pi)=L$. This is the case $\varphi=\psi=\pi$ of \cite[Theorem~2.19]{Conrad}, which describes the kernel of $\varphi\otimes\psi$ for surjective $\varphi,\psi$; for completeness we recall the argument. Clearly $\pi\otimes\pi$ is surjective and vanishes on $L$, so it induces $\alpha:(M\otimes M)/L\to Q\otimes Q$, $m\otimes m'+L\mapsto\bar m\otimes\bar m'$. Conversely, $(\bar m,\bar m')\mapsto m\otimes m'+L$ is well defined, since replacing $m,m'$ by $m+n,m'+n'$ with $n,n'\in N$ changes $m\otimes m'$ by $n\otimes m'+m\otimes n'+n\otimes n'\in L$; it is $R$-bilinear, so it induces $\beta:Q\otimes Q\to(M\otimes M)/L$ with $\beta(\bar m\otimes\bar m')=m\otimes m'+L$. As $\alpha\beta$ and $\beta\alpha$ are the identity on generators, $\alpha$ is an isomorphism and $\ker(\pi\otimes\pi)=L$. Since $(\pi\otimes\pi)(\sum_im_i\otimes m_i)=\sum_i\bar m_i\otimes\bar m_i$, we get $\sum_i\bar m_i\otimes\bar m_i=0$ if and only if $\sum_im_i\otimes m_i\in L$, so the two conditions in the lemma have the same hypothesis and the same conclusion. (If $M$ is flat, e.g.\ free, then $M\otimes N$ and $N\otimes M$ embed into $M\otimes M$ and $L=M\otimes N+N\otimes M$.)

label: thmC
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $Q:=R^n/N$. (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii) is Lemma~\ref{lem:tensorM}, as $R^n$ is flat.

(i)$\Rightarrow$(iii): If $\sum_if_{i,j}\bar f_i=0$ in $Q$ for all $j$ where $f_i=\sum_jf_{i,j}e_j$,
\[\textstyle\sum_i\bar f_i\otimes\bar f_i=\sum_j\bar e_j\otimes\sum_if_{i,j}\bar f_i=0\quad\text{in }Q\otimes Q,\]
so $\bar f_i=0$ for all $i$.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i): First, $Q$ is semiprime: if $f\in(N:f)R^n$, then $f_j\in(N:f)$ for all $j$, i.e.\ $f_jf\in N$, which is (C) for the single vector $f$; so $f\in N$. Second, $(N:f)$ is real for every $f$: if $\sum_ka_k^2f\in N$, the vectors $a_kf$ satisfy $\sum_k(a_kf_j)(a_kf)=f_j\bigl(\sum_ka_k^2f\bigr)\in N$ for all $j$, so $a_kf\in N$ by (C). Now let $f\notin N$ and let $\mathfrak p$ be a minimal prime over the real, hence radical, ideal $(N:f)=\operatorname{Ann}_R(\bar f)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:minprime}(b), $\mathfrak p$ is real, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:key}, $f\notin K(N,\mathfrak p)$. So $N=\bigcap_{\mathfrak p\text{ real}}K(N,\mathfrak p)$ is an intersection of real submodules (Lemma~\ref{lem:Kreal}), hence real.
head: environment

label: rem:ncsemi
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ncsemi}
For a noncommutative ring $R$ and a left $R$-module $M$, replace $(N:m)$ by $\langle N:m\rangle:=\{r\in R:\ rRm\subseteq N\}$, the annihilator of the submodule $R(m+N)$ of $M/N$, which is a two-sided ideal; call $N$ \emph{semiprime} if $m\in\langle N:m\rangle M$ implies $m\in N$ (the element annihilator $(N:m)$ would be too strong: for $R=M_2(k)$, $M=R$, $N=0$ and $a=E_{12}$ we have $a\in(0:a)R$, as $a^2=0$, although $0$ is semiprime in the classical sense $aRa\subseteq N\Rightarrow a\in N$). For $M=R^n$ this agrees with the definition in \cite{C22a} ``$m_iRm\subseteq N$ for $i=1,\dots,n$ implies $m\in N$'': as in \cite[Proposition~2.1]{Ary}, two-sidedness gives $\langle N:m\rangle R^n=\langle N:m\rangle^n$, so $m\in\langle N:m\rangle R^n$ if and only if $m_i\in\langle N:m\rangle$, i.e.\ $m_iRm\subseteq N$, for all $i$. For $n=1$ one recovers the classical semiprime one-sided ideals, $aRa\subseteq N\Rightarrow a\in N$ (see \cite[\ensuremath{\mathsection}1.1]{Dauns} and \cite[\ensuremath{\mathsection}1]{Sarac}), the semiprime analogue of Koh's one-sided ideals of prime type, $aRb\subseteq N\Rightarrow a\in N$ or $b\in N$ \cite{Koh}; prime submodules ($rRm\subseteq P\Rightarrow m\in P$ or $rM\subseteq P$ \cite{Dauns}) are semiprime in this sense. The semiprime submodules of \cite{Sarac} are of Dauns' type \cite[Definition~1.9(ii)]{Dauns}: $N\neq M$ and $rRrm\subseteq N$ implies $rm\in N$. Every proper semiprime submodule in our sense has this property (if $rRrm\subseteq N$, then $r\in\langle N:rm\rangle$, so $rm\in\langle N:rm\rangle M$), but not conversely, already over commutative rings \cite[Theorem~11]{JS}; for $M=R$ both notions give the semiprime left ideals.
head: environment
name: Semiprime submodules over noncommutative rings

label: rem:nc
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:nc}
Let $R$ be a $*$-ring, i.e.\ a ring with involution $*$, and $M$ a left $R$-module. The \emph{conjugate module} $M^*$ is $M$ with the right action $m\cdot r:=r^*m$, so the tensor product $M^*\otimes_RM$ of a right and a left $R$-module is defined. For noncommutative $R$ it is only an abelian group: it is generated by the $m\otimes n$ subject to biadditivity and $(r^*m)\otimes n=m\otimes rn$. Call $M$ \emph{real} if $\sum_im_i\otimes m_i=0$ in $M^*\otimes_RM$ implies $m_i=0$ for all $i$; for commutative $R$ with the trivial involution this is Definition~\ref{def:real}.

For a left ideal $I$, the map $\bar a\otimes\bar b\mapsto a^*b+(I+I^*)$ is an isomorphism of abelian groups $(R/I)^*\otimes_R(R/I)\cong R/(I+I^*)$; here $I+I^*$ is only an additive subgroup of $R$, in general neither a left nor a right ideal. Hence $R/I$ is real if and only if $\sum_ia_i^*a_i\in I+I^*$ implies $a_i\in I$ for all $i$, which is the notion of a real left ideal used in \cite{CHKMN}.

Real modules are semiprime in the sense of Remark~\ref{rem:ncsemi}. Indeed, let $q\in JM$ with $J:=\operatorname{Ann}_R(Rq)$, say $q=\sum_jb_jy_j$ with $b_j\in J$. For $b\in J$ and $r\in R$, the element $z:=b^*rq=(rq)\cdot b$ satisfies $z\otimes z=(rq)\otimes bb^*rq=0$, so $z=0$; thus $J^*\subseteq J$. Therefore $q\otimes q=\sum_j(y_j\cdot b_j^*)\otimes q=\sum_jy_j\otimes b_j^*q=0$, and $q=0$. In particular, real left ideals are semiprime. The proofs of Theorems~\ref{thmA} and \ref{thmB} rely on localization at primes and do not extend directly.

name: Real modules over $*$-rings

label: q:nc
title: Question
body_md:
\label{q:nc}
For which noncommutative rings (with involution) is every semiprime, resp.\ real, submodule an intersection of prime, resp.\ real prime, submodules?

title: Question
body_md:
\label{q:inv}
Let $R$ be commutative with a nontrivial involution. Is every real submodule, in the sense of Remark~\ref{rem:nc}, an intersection of real prime submodules?
